deride

dih-RYD · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To deride is to mock or ridicule someone or something with scorn.

Established art critics derided the young painter's first solo exhibition, calling her bold color choices childish and unrefined.

Example

For most of his rookie season, veteran players openly derided his unusual batting stance -- until his home run record silenced every critic in the clubhouse.

The veterans weren't offering constructive feedback -- they were openly mocking the rookie with contempt, exactly what deride describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ridicule: To ridicule someone is to make fun of them in a way meant to make them look foolish -- cruel laughter, not friendly joking. Deride adds open scorn and contempt: to deride is to ridicule from above, sneering down at the target as beneath serious respect.

mock: To mock is to make fun of someone or something, often by imitating them -- a voice, a walk, an accent -- and mocking can be playful or mean. Deride is never playful: it is scornful, contemptuous mockery that treats its target as worthless.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

admire: to regard with respect or approval

praise: to express warm approval of

Where it sits · how cruel the taunting becomes

tease → deride → revile

tease vs. deride: To tease someone is to make gentle, often good-natured fun of them, milder than deride.

revile vs. deride: To revile someone is to attack them with abusive, hateful language, harsher than deride.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-: down, at (Latin)

Root — ride: to laugh (from Latin ridere, 'to laugh' -- no connection to the English verb ride)

Put it together: Deride combines de- ("down, at") with ride ("to laugh," from Latin ridere -- nothing to do with riding) -- literally "to laugh down at" someone, which is exactly the scornful mockery the word describes today.

Use the root in a new word: ridiculous: My cousins argued straight through dinner about something completely ridiculous.

Root Check

Word Choice

Deride is about open, contemptuous mockery -- compare it to decry, which formally condemns something (often a policy or practice) in speech or writing, rather than laughing at it.
